newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Primakov arrives for new NATO-Russia talks.
newsitem.headline: Primakov arrives for new NATO-Russia talks.

text.p: Russian Foreign Secretary Yevgeny Primakov arrived in Brussels on Sunday for talks with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on a NATO-Russia deal to run in parallel with the alliance's eastwards expansion.
Primakov, who was met by Moscow's envoy to Belgium Vitaly Churkin, declined to speak to waiting journalists after his plane taxied to a private and secluded corner of Zaventem international airport.

Both NATO and Moscow have imposed a news blackout on the meeting, expected to take place on Sunday evening at Solana's private residence, which follows an intensive bout of diplomacy aimed at overcoming Moscow's objections to NATO enlargement.

Before the talks began, President Boris Yeltsin renewed his attack on NATO's plans to give membership to some of Moscow's former satellites, but said he thought a compromise would be reached at a summit next month with President Bill Clinton.

"We have agreed to look for a compromise and I think we will find this compromise at the summit we are holding with President Clinton on March 20-21 in Helsinki," he told reporters during his first public appearance since New Year.

Yeltsin, who discussed the issue with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Moscow last week, said his country's aim was to stall enlargement as long as possible and "not allow the renewal of confrontation".
Albright said "important progress" was made at the talks and the issue was "on the fast track".
Yeltsin's latest remarks appeared to confirm the view of several alliance diplomats who say that despite Moscow's strident public rhetoric they detected a wish by Russia to start real negotiations.

After weeks of allied concessions from arms control to offers of close military cooperation, they say Solana will now move on to the offensive and try and push Primakov to give details of what Russia can offer in return.

"Solana will push Primakov. What will Russia bring to a new relationship?," said one senior diplomat, adding Solana would try and focus the discussions on the content of any final document rather than the exact form it should take.
Russia wants a legally-binding treaty while NATO prefers a more flexible political agreement which would not need ratifying by member states' parliaments.
Last week, President Boris Yeltsin pushed the issue in a 15- minute telephone conversation with German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and later in talks with Albright.

Moscow wants the final document to contain a commitment by the allies not to place troops and weapons on the territory of new members unless they are there for internationally-approved peace-keeping operations.

NATO, committed to opposing any form of second-class membership, cannot accept outside conditions on where it positions its "infrastructure". At the same time several allies want more details of what its own military is planning.

Diplomats say Italy and France have suggested NATO examine options between a legal treaty and a political document, suggesting it may be possible to have a politically-binding agreement endorsed by governments.
